bib.title: Bad Judges of Significance (Chapter 5 of Statistics Done Wrong)

read.skipped: none; footnote reference list is not in the chapter PDF

question: Why are 'a difference in significance' and 'overlapping error bars' bad ways to judge whether two groups differ?

results.claim: If two drugs have identical nonzero effects and each trial has power B, the chance one looks significant and the other not is 2B(1-B); at 50% power that is 0.5.
results.setup: Two drugs with identical nonzero effect vs placebo, independent trials, same power B
results.quote: the probability of concluding that one drug has a signiﬁcant effect
results.note: 0.5 at B=0.5 is my arithmetic from the formula; the chapter plots it in Fig 5-1 (max 0.5 on axis).

results.claim: Boots No. 7 serum trial: 43% improved on serum vs 22% on control, called significant vs insignificant, yet the between-group difference was not significant.
results.setup: Serum vs same serum without active ingredient, 2007 trial
results.quote: the serum reduced the number of wrinkles in 43%

results.claim: Neuroscientists use the incorrect (difference-in-significance) method for comparing groups about half the time.
results.quote: use the incorrect method for comparing groups about half

results.claim: Five statin meta-analyses (3 'yes', 2 'inconclusive') all gave relative risk of mortality near 0.9, i.e. about 10% fewer deaths, so they did not really disagree.
results.setup: Statins in patients with no history of cardiovascular disease
results.quote: the relative risk estimates were all near
results.note: Quote continues on next line: '0.9, indicating that during the trial periods, 10% fewer patients'

results.claim: Fixitol vs Solvix example: 95% CIs overlap yet a t test gives p < 0.05, so overlap-checking is stricter than p < 0.05.
results.setup: Two groups of 10 patients, time to recovery, bars assumed to be 95% CIs (Fig 5-3); underlying numbers not given
results.quote: signiﬁcant difference between them, even though the conﬁdence intervals
results.note: p computed on unpublished numbers; value stated only as inequality

results.claim: A standard error bar is about half as wide as a 95% CI, so papers labelled 'standard error' may actually show 2 SE.

A survey found most psychologists, neuroscientists and medical researchers judged significance by CI overlap, and a climate-science survey found most papers comparing two groups with error bars made this error.
results.source: footnotes 7 and 8 (not named in chapter text)
results.setup: Surveys of published papers and researchers

limits: Chapter gives no data for Fixitol/Solvix; they are invented illustrations.
The 2006 older-brothers study could not be re-tested because the paper did not publish enough data.
Visual-comparison procedures such as Gabriel comparison intervals require equal standard deviations in each group.
Comparing directly does not improve power; it only avoids the false conclusion that drugs differ.
practices: Compare groups directly with an appropriate test, or a CI for the difference, instead of saying one was significant and one was not (p.56, Tips p.62).
Test whether the difference is significant rather than looking for a difference in significance (p.56).
Do not judge significance by eye from overlapping CIs or SE bars; use a hypothesis test (p.61-62).
Visual CI check is valid only against a fixed value such as zero (p.61).
State whether error bars are SD, SE or 95% CI (p.60).
Adjust for multiple comparisons when comparing many groups; Bonferroni is tedious and conservative (p.62).
Read replication failures as possibly consistent with the original given truth inflation and lower true power (p.57).
